After my colleague Tony Polanco wrapped up his Acer Googlebook 14 review, he handed over the 2-in-1 convertible to me to put it through its paces and see what an Android phone power user thinks of Google’s new computing platform. One of the reasons a Googlebook appeals to me is how seamlessly it supposedly works with your Android phone, while offering you a rich desktop experience.

I know a lot about that PC-like experience, having tested some of the best Android phones and their desktop interfaces — namely Samsung DeX on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Android 17 desktop mode with Pixel phones, and Lenovo’s Smart Connect on the Motorola Razr Fold. These are features that I like to refer to as an extension of my phone, mainly because of how they deliver that desktop experience when connected to external devices like a monitor or AR glasses.

After spending over three weeks with the Acer Googlebook 14, I learned a lot about the platform, including its advantages and disadvantages over using my Android phone with a desktop mode. Here’s what I found.

The Acer Googlebook 14 is a 2-in-1 convertible laptop that bridges the gap between mobile and desktop productivity, packing a crisp 14-inch display, Intel Core Ultra 5 (Series 3) processor, and full Chrome extension support. With multi-user profiles, virtual workspaces, and seamless access to Android apps right out of the box, it’s an ideal everyday workhorse.

As much as I love falling back on DeX when I accidentally leave my laptop at home, I get annoyed that Samsung still refuses to bring back support for multiple users. This isn’t an issue with the Acer Googlebook 14, as it lets me set up separate user accounts — each with its own unique lock code and personalized desktop.

This is perfect because I would rather keep my work and personal accounts separate, and it’s also useful if you intend on letting your kids or other people access the laptop. That isn’t an option with Samsung DeX, which is one of its biggest limitations, though the Pixel’s desktop mode does let me switch profiles.

While the Acer Googlebook 14 handles basic multitasking well enough, its proper side-by-side window snapping is restricted to just two apps at a time — effectively making it no different from any phone desktop mode.

I appreciate how smoothly both windows resize in tandem when dragging the center border slider, which makes it easy to prioritize a browser window next to Slack while I’m working. However, as someone who regularly juggles multiple apps at once, I would much rather be able to pin up to four apps simultaneously in a grid.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I use Chrome all the time, especially for doing work-related tasks. While I can lean on a phone desktop mode for most things related to Chrome, there’s simply one thing I cannot do: access the handful of Chrome extensions that are crucial for working with a content management system (CMS).

With the Acer Googlebook 14, I can run the exact same desktop Chrome extensions I rely on for work, including price-checking tools, grammar checkers, link generators, and more. Having those tools built directly into the browser makes it feel more like a true laptop replacement.

I’m more productive on a Googlebook than with my phone’s desktop mode thanks to how it supports multiple virtual desktops and virtually limitless apps. The beauty of having up to four desktops is that I can organize them based on my workflow — like keeping one dedicated to spreadsheets, another to social media, and the rest to all of my work-related apps.

Even though phone desktop modes also offer several desktops for me to organize, their main limitation is that they’re normally capped at five apps. This isn’t a major disadvantage per se, but having access to far more on a Googlebook is helpful when I need it.

Despite Googlebook OS running on an Android foundation, I was surprised to discover that not every Android app from the Google Play Store is available for me to install. Several staples I rely on daily — including Amazon, Twitter/X, and CyberLink’s PowerDirector — simply aren’t available just yet.

I suspect it’s simply a matter of these developers optimizing their apps for this new laptop form factor. While I can easily fall back on the web versions for shopping on Amazon or scrolling through X, losing native access to a full-featured video editor like PowerDirector is a real setback. In contrast, when I use Samsung DeX or Pixel’s desktop mode, every app already installed on my phone is immediately accessible.

After putting in serious time with the Acer Googlebook 14, it’s clear that Googlebook OS has distinct advantages over phone desktop modes like Samsung DeX and Android 17’s native desktop experience.

With full Chrome extension support, multiple virtual workspaces, and multi-user profile switching, I’m noticeably more productive on it than when working off a docked phone. However, there’s still room for improvement — particularly around app availability gaps and window-snapping limitations — before it can permanently replace my Windows laptop.

#3180. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3177. These TP-Link Routers Are up to $100 Off in Amazon's Early Black Friday Sale

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Black Friday isn't until November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some decent discounts on TP-Link routers, with prices starting at $44.99 and savings of up to $100. The deals cover quite a few different networking needs, from compact travel routers that let you connect multiple devices to hotel wifi to more powerful home routers designed for faster internet plans and households with lots of connected devices.

TP-Link’s Roam routers are compact enough to travel with and let you share a hotel or public internet connection across your devices through a private Wi-Fi network—and right now, Amazon has three models on sale: the Roam 6 AX1500 for $44.99 (was $59.99), the Roam 6 AX3000 for $55.98 (was $79.99), and the Roam 7 BE3600 for $87.99 (was $119.99). All three support VPN connections and multiple operating modes, with the main differences coming down to speed. The AX1500 offers up to 1.5Gbps, the AX3000 doubles that and adds a 2.5Gbps WAN port, while the Wi-Fi 7-enabled Roam 7 reaches up to 3.6Gbps.

The TP-Link Archer AX21 V5 AX1800 is down to $54.99 from $89.99, saving you $35 on an affordable Wi-Fi 6 router for everyday home use. Its dual-band connection offers combined theoretical speeds of up to 1.8Gbps, which should be sufficient for typical activities like streaming, video calls, and browsing across several devices.

For homes with faster internet plans, multiple gamers, or lots of connected devices, TP-Link's Archer BE700 and BE770 offer tri-band Wi-Fi 7, including access to the 6GHz band for compatible devices. Both support EasyMesh for extended coverage and have 10Gbps WAN ports, although the BE770 provides faster wireless speeds and more wired connectivity. As for pricing, the TP-Link Archer BE700 is down to $248 from $349.99, saving you just over $100. It offers theoretical speeds of up to 15Gbps, a 2.5Gbps LAN port, and three Gigabit LAN ports. For just $52 more, the Archer BE770 (now $299.99, was $369.99) bumps speeds up to 18Gbps and adds a dedicated 10Gbps LAN port, making it better suited to high-speed network storage and large file transfers.

The TP-Link Deco BE25 is down to $99.98 from $129.99, saving you $30 on a Wi-Fi 7 router designed to work as part of a mesh network. It offers dual-band wireless speeds of up to 5Gbps, two 2.5Gbps Ethernet ports, and AI-driven roaming that helps connected devices switch between Deco units as you move around your home.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

#3176. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

'The End of Oak Street,' 'Other Mommy,' 'Heartland,' and more movie night hits just landed on streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Another weekend is here, and with it comes tons of new options for what to watch across the best streaming services. I'm here every weekend shouting out which new movies on streaming are worth adding to your queue. This week, Jessica Chaplain is coming for our watchlist with two marquee films: Netflix's latest neo-noir mystery "Heartland" and the unsettling and campy "Other Mommy" on paid video-on-demand platforms.

For an easy crowd-pleaser for family movie night, look no further than "The End of Oak Street" on HBO Max, one of Anne Hathaway's many stellar performances this year. Over on Apple TV Plus, you'll find an irreverent and inspirational drama about speaking truth to power in "Being Heumann." Or if you'd rather keep the spirit of spooky season alive a little longer (who could blame you), Netflix just got the psychological horror movie "Smile" that'll really mess with your head.

So without further ado, let's dive into the best new movies to watch this weekend.

If you liked: "Super 8," "Jumanji," "The Mist,"

From David Robert Mitchell, the writer-director behind cult horror hit and one of my favorite movies "It Follows," comes a swing for the fences with this chaotic dinosaur adventure that doesn't take itself too seriously. Set in a quiet 1982 suburb, "The End of Oak Street" follows the Platt family, led by Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor).

They're propelled by the narrative into a "Jurassic Park" style nightmare when their entire neighborhood gets warped into a prehistoric world. Now stranded and surrounded by apex predators, the family and their neighbors must put aside their differences and work together if they hope to survive. For a fun 99-minute shot in the arm of nostalgia this weekend, you could do far worse than this Spielbergian fever dream.

Watch "The End of Oak Street" on HBO Max now

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

If you liked: "Chinatown," any of Taylor Sheridan's shows

Jessica Chastain continues her streak as one of Hollywood's most bankable actors in Netflix's "Heartland," playing a former country star turned detective searching for her niece. A neo-noir mystery from writer-director Shana Feste ("Country Strong," "The Greatest"), "Heartland" sees the reclusive singer Misty Jones (Chastain) whisked back to Nashville to explore its darker corners while confronting her own troubled past.

The ever-prickly Misty speedruns one girl failure after another, all spit and vinegar as the slow drip of clues takes her to an old ex (Ross Lynch) and a seedy manager in Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund). With an Oscar-winner in the lead role is a huge draw, and its promising 82% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes and #1 spot in the Netflix Top 10, "Heartland" has all the makings of this weekend's biggest hit.

If you liked: "Coraline," "Host," "The Babadook"

If one Jessica Chastain movie wasn't enough for you, by do I have news for you. Her unnerving supernatural horror flick "The Other Mommy" is available to rent or purchase this weekend. If it were me, I'd wait until it comes to Peacock (likely around February), but this one was a lot of fun when I saw it in theaters. Director Rob Savage ("Host") leans into his horror roots with plenty of jump scares, grotesque transformations and scenes that will haunt your nightmares.

Chastain also looks like she's having a blast pulling double duty as both the loving, picture-perfect mom and her demonic lookalike. Seven-year-old Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) has an imaginary friend that's anything but harmless. A sinister shape-shifter known as Other Mommy emerges from her closet, taking on the appearance of Bela's mother (Chastain) and pleading to be let into her heart. As the creature's threats become increasingly terrifying, Bela's parents (Jay Duplass and Chastain) do everything they can to keep their daughter safe.

Buy or rent "The Other Mommy" on Amazon or Apple

If you liked: "Then Barbara Met Alan," "Music Within," "Coda"

"Being Heumann" is one of those movies that restores your faith in humanity for a while yet. "CODA" director Siân Heder brings this remarkable true story to the screen about a group of people who, when there was no seat for them at the table, forged their own. In 1977, disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) leads a coalition of frustrated protesters in a 28-day occupation of a San Francisco federal building.

Their demand? That the government finally enforce their civil rights under Section 504. Mark Ruffalo plays the bureaucrat standing in their way, with Dylan O'Brien as a reporter on the ground while history is made. It'd take a heart of stone not to be moved by Madeley's fiery performance here; Heumann ain't exactly winning any popularity contests, but she surges with the kind of infectious spirit needed to bring about meaningful change.

If you liked: "Oculus," "The Ritual," "Black Phone" (also all on Netflix)

Spooky season may be over, but Netflix has a particularly stellar crop of horror movies right now, including one of my favorites that got added this month: "Smile." It's a thoroughly unnerving ride that leverages horror movie tropes to screw with your head and land some solid scares.

Sosie Bacon stars as Rose, a therapist at a psychiatric ward in New Jersey who, in the movie's opening moments, witness a new patient kill herself with an eerie smile on her face. That kicks off a curse that stalks her relentlessly, one smiling stranger at a time. With all her friends and family writing her off as a mental breakdown in progress, she'll have to carve her way out of this nightmare on her own.

#3173. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Soundbars From Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3172. Bowen Yang Returns To ‘Saturday Night Live’ As Jensen Huang In Cold Open That Skewers Tech Billionaires’ Susceptibility To Honey Pot Plots

Bowen Yang returned to Saturday Night Live to play Jensen Huang in the show’s cold open, a skewering of tech billionaires susceptibility to honey pots, or being wooed by attractive women and thinking that they genuinely are in it for the romance.

The skit follows Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia following revelations that he had an affair with a woman who may have been a Chinese spy, and another affair with a subordinate. That sent shares of the company tumbling.

“When you invite Jensen over, you know what is about to go down — the S&P 500,” Yang’s Huang said. “That’s right — I’m into BDSM — breaking da stock market.” Related Stories News Shane Gillis Addresses 'SNL' Monologue After He Promised Show "No Controversy" News Donald Trump Urges Congress To Pass Federal Film & TV Tax Incentive Amid Worries Bill Will Languish: "Get This Done!"

The premise of the skit had John Mulaney, this week’s host, playing a CIA official trying to instruct the gathered tech billionaires to be on the lookout for women who show interest in them. Watch on Deadline

“America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy,” the CIA official told them. “Now you all saw former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resined this week after he was acught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. What do you think the lesson is here?”

“Yeah, never date a Chinese woman,” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline) answered.

“Never date a human,” said Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes).

“Never date anyone lest they become the Antichrist,” responded Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson).

“No, and Peter, you go to chill with the Antichrist stuff,” the CIA official told him.

The recent midterms in many ways were a backlash against the AI overlords, with opposition to data centers reflecting fears of AI’s impact on jobs and humanity.

“Show us some respect. We do a lot for this country,” Thiel told the CIA official. “Name one time technology has let us down.”

“Yesterday, when every plane in America was grounded,” the CIA official answered.

“The day before that, when Microsoft went dark,” the CIA official reminded.

Mulaney’s character went on, “Look, I get it, I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you to go from these bug-eyed little weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and strange as you, a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

The skit also featured Ben Marhsall as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Jeremy Culhane’s return as an Elon Musk, incomprehensible to the point where the CIA official has to spray him with a water bottle to shut him up.

The CIA official tried to get across the dangers they were facing in getting hooked in to a spy plot.

“Let’s start an exercise,” the CIA official told them. “Let’s say you’re at a bar and an attractive woman approaches and asks you, ‘What are you working on?’ Dario, what do you say?”

Amodei responded, “I would say, ‘Madam, what a pleasure to see you this evening. May I interest you in an industry secret?'”

Zuckerberg then said, “I would just assume that she wanted to sleep with the man who created the metaverse, as all woman do.”

“But they don’t, right?” the CIA official said, before showing him a Venn diagram. Next to a large circle of beautiful women was a tiny dot representing “people who like the metaverse.”

#3171. Microsoft Outlook experiencing widespread outage

Everybody’s working for the weekend, but Microsoft Outlook clocked out early. The mission-critical email service is facing a widespread outage.

The outage appears to have started about an hour ago. Based on status checks with the service, the issue is widespread and ongoing.

Downdetector reports over a hundred thousand Outlook outage reports today.

If you’re having trouble with Microsoft Outage, err.. Outlook, you’re not alone.

Usually you can check the latest Outlook outage status here, although it appears to maybe be down as well.

Update: Here’s a status update from Microsoft:

We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. As a precaution, we’ve paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event. We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure. We’re investigating what’s causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service.

#3170. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3169. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

Experts think it typically takes three to four weeks for the body to recover after running a marathon, but what does the tech say? To find out more, I looked at my readiness scores on three different wearables the morning after the marathon and for the next few days — read on to find out more.

Before we dive into the data, a reminder that you can read my Apple Watch Ultra 4 review, Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review, and Oura Ring 5 review here on Tom’s Guide.

For the race, I wore my Apple Watch Ultra 4 on one wrist and my Garmin Fenix 9 Pro on the other: you can read which was more accurate here. I also had my Oura Ring 5 on my index finger for both the race and the post-race celebrations.

Despite sleeping well the night before the race, with the clocks changing giving me an extra hour of sleep before I took on my seventh marathon in the wind and rain, the night of the marathon was a different story.

Sure, my legs were tired, and I’d spent a few hours in the pub celebrating, but at 2 am I was wide awake and struggled to get back to sleep. My legs were twitching, and I could tell wine and chips probably wasn’t the best recovery move.

The next morning, it wasn’t a pretty picture when I downloaded my data. My Oura Ring 5 gave me a readiness score of 35/100. “Your resting heart rate trend indicates that your body might be strained at the moment,” it told me. My sleep score was 45/100, with only 4 hours and 52 minutes of sleep. It also said I needed to pay attention to the amount of activity I’d had the previous day.

Apple also flagged that things were slightly off, giving me a readiness score of 3/10 (why Apple decided on a Readiness score out of 10, not 100, will always confuse me). The overnight vitals showed that while my wrist temperature was typical, my heart rate and respiratory rate were elevated. My recovery HRV the next day also showed there was stress on my body.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Garmin told a similar story: the night before I went to bed, my Fenix 9 Pro told me my overall stress level was 60 and that my body battery was at -64, which felt about right as I lay down on my paper-thin pillow in possibly the worst hotel I’ve ever stayed in. The next morning, my Training Readiness score was 25/100 — in the Poor bracket. I’ve always found Garmin the most brutal when it comes to evaluating my performance, and it was the same here.

So what do I do with all of this data? I was in no fit state to run the next morning or for the following week, but I found it interesting to look at the different scores and how each wearable understood what was happening.

My Garmin seemed to grasp that my recovery was down to the previous day’s efforts, my Oura focused on a bad night’s sleep being “normal for parents and at this stage in my cycle,” and Apple, as always, didn’t go much further other than flagging that I should “pace myself.”

It’s also worth noting that, looking at my Oura Ring and Apple Watch data for the entire week following the race, my readiness scores hovered around 60/100, 6/10 mark. My resting heart rate remained elevated as my body recovered and I fought off the cold my toddler gave me the second I walked in the door, and it took me a few days to catch up on the sleep I’d missed.

While I still believe in listening to your body more than any wearable device, it’s interesting to see the toll a major workout has on your sleep, heart rate, and recovery.

#3167. iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

#3166. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3165. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3162. The Apple Watch Series 11 Is $100 Off in Walmart's Early Black Friday Sale

If you’ve been counting down to Black Friday and hoping for a deal on an Apple Watch, there’s no time like the present: Walmart recently launched its early Black Friday tech deals, and the rarely discounted Apple Watch Series 11 is currently $100 off, bringing the 42mm GPS model down to $299 (originally $399). The 46mm GPS model is $329 (originally $429), while the GPS + Cellular versions start at $399 and are also $100 off.

Though it has been supplanted by the Series 12, released earlier this fall, the Series 11 is still a great buy.
